thesis: Isaac Newton set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and developed calculus, the mathematics of change. Training a neural network is a calculus problem: gradient descent follows slopes to nudge millions of weights downhill, and momentum treats them like a rolling Newtonian ball.

story.title: A cannon on a mountain
story.text: Newton realised that the pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon. In a thought experiment published with the Principia, he imagined firing a cannon sideways from a very high mountain. A slow ball falls nearby. Each faster ball lands further away, until one falls so far that the curved ground drops away beneath it. It never lands. That is an orbit.

story.title: Falling all the way round
story.text: Newton's law of gravity can be worked out in small steps: find the pull toward the Earth's centre, nudge the velocity by it, move, and repeat. From a high mountain, a ball slower than about 7.9 km/s hits the ground, one at that speed circles, and one faster than about 11.2 km/s escapes. Stronger gravity raises both speeds.

story.title: The same nudge trains AI
story.text: Neural networks learn by gradient descent: find the slope of the error and nudge every weight downhill. Adding momentum, popularised for backpropagation in 1986, makes the rule look exactly like the cannonball's: velocity gets nudged by the slope, then position by velocity. The weights roll, overshoot and settle at the minimum.

hint: Slide the launch speed from 3 to 13 km/s and watch the apple fall back, circle the Earth, stretch into an ellipse and finally escape; then raise gravity and find the new orbit speed.
